question_title: Will a U.S. federal agency announce new or expanded model evaluation agreements with both OpenAI and Anthropic before September 3, 2026?
summary:
Resolves YES only if a U.S. federal AGENCY OFFICIALLY ANNOUNCES, strictly between Aug 10 and Sept 3 2026, new or materially expanded voluntary agreements to evaluate frontier models from BOTH OpenAI and Anthropic. Status quo is NO.

The decisive structural fact is that the biggest relevant event sits just outside the window. EO 14409 (June 2, 2026) mandated a voluntary pre-release review framework; it was finalized around the Aug 1 deadline and the White House convened ~a dozen labs — including OpenAI and Anthropic — on Aug 4 to "close the loop." That was the natural announcement moment, it occurred before Aug 10, and it produced no public agency announcement. Instead, Fortune and Axios reported on Aug 4 that the White House has no plans to publicly release the framework; participation details stay "under wraps, only known to a select group of companies." WSJ reported CAISI was directed to stop publishing model assessments. The Aug 1 statutory deliverables lapsed with zero public output. CAISI has had no permanent director since July 20 (NIST's Arvind Raman is dual-hatted as acting head).

I checked the pre-publication trap explicitly: the window start (Aug 10) precedes published_at (Aug 15), so this is Case 1 and an Aug 10-15 event would legitimately count — I searched for one and found nothing.

The strongest counter-precedent is the one the question's own background cites. On May 5, 2026 CAISI did issue a formal agreements release — but it named Google DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI, while the OpenAI/Anthropic renegotiations surfaced only via Bloomberg, never an official release naming them. That is exactly this question's failure mode: real activity, no qualifying official announcement. Compounding it, a White House official says the framework already covers OpenAI's and Anthropic's closed models, with the advertised next expansion aimed at open-weight developers — so the modal next announcement adds different companies.

Quantitatively I decomposed rather than argued narratively: P(any genre announcement in the 24-day window) × P(covers both | announcement) × P(clears the "materially expanded" fine print), plus an additive lenient-resolution allowance for a NIST informational post like the ~Aug 2025 "CAISI Works with OpenAI and Anthropic" page. Monte Carlo center ≈ 4.5%; sensitivity across secrecy multiplier 0.25-0.60, activity multiplier 1.8-3.0, p_both 0.25-0.45 and leniency 0.02-0.08 gives 2.5-6.9% — stable, not knife-edge. Anchor (−2.94) plus factor sum (−0.53) implies ≈3%.

I settle at 6%, above both the factor sum and the simulation center, conceding the premortem's two strongest points: CAISI kept issuing partnership-type announcements (July 2026 Kimi K3 assessment, OpenMined CRADA, GSA MOU) even while assessment reporting was curbed, so the secrecy read was over-broad; and EO 14409 creates genuinely new paperwork that would qualify as a previously-not-covered access arrangement. The main known weakness is that government press pages rendered as empty shells and no date-filtered news search was available, so my "nothing in Aug 10-19" is softer evidence than I would like.

Fortune (Aug 4, 2026): 'White House won't publicly release AI model evaluation framework it reviewed today with Meta, Nvidia, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic' — details 'kept under wraps, only known to a select group of companies that may choose to participate.' Axios (Aug 4): 'White House plans to keep AI framework under wraps'; benchmarks/thresholds classified. WSJ: days after EO 14409 the administration directed CAISI to stop issuing public reports of its model assessments. The Aug 1 EO deadline lapsed with zero public deliverables (no Federal Register notices, no NIST/CISA publications, no OSTP statements). Downweighted from my initial read because CAISI kept publishing partnership-type items (July 2026 Kimi K3 joint assessment, OpenMined CRADA, GSA MOU) — the curb targeted model assessments, not all announcements.

Elevated activity environment: EO 14409 (June 2, 2026) mandated a voluntary pre-release review framework; it was finalized around the Aug 1 deadline and ~a dozen labs were briefed at a White House 'close the loop' meeting on Aug 4. The program is entering implementation/enrollment, and every participating lab must paper its participation under a new instrument — mechanically raising the hazard of a qualifying announcement versus a quiet baseline.

Wrong expansion vector. Per a White House official, the framework 'currently applies only to closed models from Anthropic and OpenAI,' and the advertised next expansion is toward open-weight models (Meta, Nvidia) once they reach frontier level. The May 5, 2026 CAISI release is a counter-precedent rather than a supporting one: it officially named Google DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI, while the OpenAI/Anthropic renegotiations surfaced only through Bloomberg reporting, never an official release naming them. That is precisely this question's failure mode — real activity, no official announcement covering both.

Revealed preference at the natural announcement moment, plus elapsed time. The Aug 3-4 framework finalization and lab briefing — the single most likely trigger for an agreements announcement — produced no public agency announcement, and falls before the Aug 10 window start so cannot resolve the question (the window appears drawn deliberately to exclude it). 9 of the 24 window days (Aug 10-19) have elapsed with nothing qualifying found across many query formulations.

Degraded CAISI institutional capacity: director Chris Fall resigned July 20, 2026 after ~3 months; NIST Director Arvind Raman is dual-hatted as acting head while a permanent successor is sought; Rep. Khanna has publicly flagged the vacuum. Leaderless agencies issue fewer flagship announcements, and late August is a DC recess lull.

Countervailing pressure toward disclosure: Senate Democrats' letter calls the strategy 'ad-hoc and unpredictable' and demands an unclassified response on model-access policy; The Hill reports the closed-door framework blindsided the policy sector. Announcing that agreements exist (while keeping contents classified) is a cheap, direct rebuttal, and both labs publicly lobbied for the 30-day review and would welcome credit.

Lenient-resolution pathway: NIST previously posted a non-press-release page ('CAISI Works with OpenAI and Anthropic to Promote Secure AI Innovation', ~Aug 2025) describing joint security evaluation work with both labs alongside UK AISI. A similar post, or agency confirmation accompanying paired company blog posts, could be read as a 'materially expanded' evaluation domain. This is the single largest YES contributor in my Monte Carlo.

Verification weakness (widens uncertainty, mild net negative given status-quo default). Primary sources were largely unreadable: nist.gov/caisi and the NIST news search returned JS-rendered shells, the August 2026 news index 404'd, and no date-filtered news search was available. My 'nothing found in Aug 10-19' rests on generic web search, so absence of evidence is weaker here than usual — though six independent query angles all returned the same May and early-August items.

## Reasoning

**What must happen:** A U.S. federal *agency* must *officially announce*, strictly between Aug 10 and Sept 3, 2026, new or materially expanded voluntary agreements to evaluate frontier models from **both** OpenAI and Anthropic.

**The decisive finding:** The biggest relevant event falls just *outside* the window. EO 14409 (June 2, 2026) mandated a voluntary pre-release review framework; it was finalized around its Aug 1 deadline, and the White House convened ~a dozen labs — including OpenAI and Anthropic — on **Aug 4** to "close the loop." That was the natural announcement moment, it preceded Aug 10, and it produced no public agency announcement. Instead:

- Fortune and Axios (Aug 4): the White House has **no plans to publicly release** the framework — details stay "under wraps, only known to a select group of companies"
- WSJ: CAISI was directed to **stop publishing** model assessments
- The Aug 1 EO deliverables lapsed with zero public output (no Federal Register notices, no NIST/CISA publications)
- CAISI has had **no permanent director** since July 20; NIST's Arvind Raman is dual-hatted as acting head

**The strongest counter-precedent is the question's own background.** On May 5, 2026 CAISI *did* issue a formal agreements release — but it named Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and xAI. The OpenAI/Anthropic renegotiations surfaced only via Bloomberg, never an official release naming them. That is precisely this question's failure mode: real activity, no qualifying official announcement. A White House official also states the framework *already* covers both labs' closed models, with the next expansion aimed at open-weight developers — so the modal next announcement adds different companies.

**Method:** I decomposed rather than argued narratively — P(any genre announcement) × P(covers both) × P(clears the "materially expanded" fine print), plus an allowance for lenient resolution via a NIST informational post like the ~Aug 2025 "CAISI Works with OpenAI and Anthropic" page. Monte Carlo center ≈4.5%; sensitivity across four parameters gives 2.5–6.9%, so the estimate is stable rather than knife-edge.

I landed at 6% — above both my factor sum (~3%) and simulation center — conceding two points from my own premortem: CAISI *did* keep issuing partnership-type announcements (July's Kimi K3 assessment, an OpenMined CRADA, a GSA MOU) even while assessment reporting was curbed, so my secrecy read was over-broad; and EO 14409 creates genuinely new paperwork that would qualify as a previously-uncovered access arrangement.

**Two caveats worth stating plainly.** First, I verified the Aug 10–19 stretch only through generic web search — `nist.gov/caisi` and the NIST news search returned JavaScript shells, the August 2026 news index 404'd, and no date-filtered news tool was available. Six query angles all returned the same May and early-August items, but a GovDelivery bulletin from mid-August could plausibly have escaped me. Second, the `research()` tool failed twice: once with a sub-agent contract error, and once by writing a 64k-character result to a path outside my read allowlist — I recovered by gathering everything directly.

input.assessment:
STEP 1 PARSE. Resolves YES only if, strictly between Aug 10 and Sept 3, 2026 ET, a U.S. FEDERAL AGENCY OFFICIALLY ANNOUNCES new or materially expanded voluntary agreements under which a federal agency evaluates frontier models from BOTH OpenAI and Anthropic for an explicitly identified frontier-model security risk. Announcer must be an agency (company blog posts alone don't suffice). Fine print: separate announcements OK, but expansions count only if they identify a previously-not-covered model family, access arrangement, testing scope, or evaluation domain. Status quo = NO.

PRE-PUBLICATION TRAP CHECK: The criteria specify an explicit start date (Aug 10) that PRECEDES published_at (Aug 15) — this is Step 1b Case 1, so an Aug 10-15 event would legitimately count. I searched for one and found nothing. Critically, the biggest recent event — framework finalization plus the White House 'close the loop' meeting with Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, Nvidia — occurred Aug 3-4, BEFORE the window, so it cannot resolve YES. The window appears deliberately drawn to exclude it.

THE CORE TENSION. Two forces point opposite ways. (1) Activity is unusually high: EO 14409 (June 2, 2026) mandated a voluntary pre-release review framework; it was finalized around the Aug 1 deadline; labs were briefed Aug 4; implementation is beginning. In a normal world that raises the odds of a follow-on agency announcement. (2) But this specific program has an explicitly documented anti-publication posture. Fortune and Axios both reported on Aug 4 that the White House has NO plans to publicly release the framework — details stay 'under wraps, only known to a select group of companies.' Benchmarks and covered-model thresholds are classified. WSJ reported CAISI was told to stop publishing its model assessments. The Aug 1 statutory deliverables lapsed with zero public output. Force (2) is much better evidenced and directly targets the observable the question requires — a public agency announcement.

WHY THE 'BOTH' REQUIREMENT BITES. Even conditional on some announcement, it likely won't name these two. A White House official stated the framework already applies to OpenAI's and Anthropic's closed models; the advertised expansion direction is toward open-weight models once they reach frontier level. The May 5, 2026 CAISI release is the template for a qualifying announcement — and it named Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and xAI, with OpenAI/Anthropic renegotiations surfacing only via Bloomberg reporting, not an official release. That is precisely the failure mode here: real activity, no official announcement naming both.

QUANTIFICATION. Monte Carlo decomposition: P(any genre announcement in window) × P(covers both | announcement) × P(meets 'materially expanded' fine print) + additive lenient-resolution allowance. Baseline genre rate 0.8-2.0/yr over a 24/365 window, multiplied by an activity uplift (~2.2×) and a secrecy suppressor (~0.30×); p_both ~ Beta(3.5,6.5) mean 0.35; p_material ~ Beta(6,4) mean 0.60. Core ≈ 1.5%; with the lenient pathway ≈ 3.9%. Sensitivity grid over secrecy multiplier 0.25-0.60 and activity multiplier 1.8-3.0 gives a total range of 3.5%-6.4% (mean 4.6%); varying p_both (0.25-0.45) and the lenient probability (0.02-0.08) gives 2.5%-6.9%. The estimate is stable — it does not swing wildly under reasonable reparameterization.

NO SCENARIO (concrete, ~95%): The framework stays classified. Companies participate quietly under the already-existing arrangements. CAISI, still under an acting dual-hatted director, publishes nothing about OpenAI or Anthropic through Sept 3. Congress keeps complaining; the administration keeps declining to disclose. Question resolves NO.

YES SCENARIO (concrete, ~5%): Congressional pressure or a competitive-messaging impulse flips the calculus — Commerce/NIST issues a May-5-style release announcing that OpenAI and Anthropic have signed expanded agreements covering the new EO 14409 classified cyber-benchmarking domain (a genuinely previously-not-covered evaluation domain, so it clears the fine print). Alternatively NIST posts an 'CAISI Works with OpenAI and Anthropic' style update naming a new testing scope and the resolver counts it.

FINAL. I take 5%, at the upper-middle of the simulation range and above the strict factor-sum implication (~3%), because the policy environment is genuinely in flux and I want to respect the possibility of a surprise announcement in an active implementation phase. This is not a hedge toward 50% — it is a small upward allowance for model uncertainty on a question whose status quo is firmly NO.
input.calibration_notes: Anchor 5% (logit -2.94) from the historical rate of qualifying announcements naming both labs (~1/yr over 24 months, scaled to a 24-day window). Final estimate 5% — essentially at anchor, but that masks real movement underneath: a strong negative cluster (documented non-publication policy, CAISI ordered to stop public reporting, leaderless agency, Aug 1 deliverables lapsed, 9 of 24 days already elapsed with nothing) is nearly offset by a genuine positive (the framework just finalized and implementation/enrollment is live, plus a lenient-resolution pathway with precedent). Strict factor-sum implies ~3%; my Monte Carlo center is ~4.5%; sensitivity range 2.5-6.9%. I chose 5%, slightly above the factor sum, as an explicit allowance for surprise in an actively moving policy environment. HEDGING CHECK: not applicable — 5% is a committed, non-central position. STATUS QUO CHECK: applies with full force; this is a predictive question requiring an affirmative public event in a short window, and the dramatic/newsworthy YES outcome is exactly the kind forecasters overweight. PRECEDENT CHECK: I ran the four-step test on the May 5, 2026 CAISI announcement, which is the tempting precedent. Its causal conditions do NOT hold now — it happened under a permanent CAISI director, before EO 14409 centralized the program under Treasury/NSA/CISA, and before the administration adopted an explicit non-publication posture. And the counter-precedent is decisive: that very announcement covered the other three labs while OpenAI's and Anthropic's renegotiations surfaced only through Bloomberg, never an official release naming them.
input.key_uncertainties: (1) Biggest unknown: whether a qualifying announcement already occurred between Aug 10 and Aug 19 that my searches missed. Government press pages rendered as empty JS shells and I have no date-filtered news search, so my 'nothing found' is weaker evidence than I would like — though I probed it from six different query angles. (2) How strictly the resolver reads 'officially announces.' If paired OpenAI and Anthropic blog posts about federal evaluation work, or a NIST informational page rather than a press release, are counted, YES probability roughly doubles. If only a formal agency press release counts, it drops toward 2-3%. (3) Whether the classified EO 14409 cyber-benchmarking regime would be characterized publicly at all — if it is, it plausibly constitutes a 'previously not-covered evaluation domain' and would clear the fine print easily. (4) I could not read the WSJ, Axios, or Bloomberg originals directly (paywalls/403), so several load-bearing facts about the secrecy posture come via secondary characterization in TechPolicy.Press and Fortune. I consider the secrecy finding well-corroborated across independent outlets, but not primary-sourced.

input.update_triggers: Would move me UP sharply (+15pp or more): a nist.gov/news-events or Commerce press release, or a GovDelivery USNIST bulletin, dated Aug 10-Sep 3 with 'OpenAI' and/or 'Anthropic' in the title alongside 'agreement'/'evaluation'; a White House reversal announcing publication of the EO 14409 framework together with a named participant roster; a named permanent CAISI director installed and making a debut agreements announcement; simultaneous OpenAI and Anthropic posts about a NEW federal evaluation domain that NIST or OSTP officially confirms. Would move me DOWN (-2pp, toward 3%): explicit reiteration by OSTP or Commerce that participant identities and framework terms remain classified; passage of Sept 3 approaching with continued silence; confirmation that the next expansion tranche targets open-weight developers (Meta, Nvidia) rather than OpenAI/Anthropic.
input.process_reflection:
The research() tool was the main friction point and it failed in two distinct ways in one session. The first failure ('turn completed without a valid submit_output call') is a sub-agent contract violation. The second is worse and is a plain scaffolding bug: the tool wrote a 64k-char payload to /tmp/aib-agent-cwd/.lup/... and told me to go read it in chunks, but that path is not in my Read allowlist, so the tool handed me a pointer to data I am structurally forbidden from opening. Large research payloads should be written into the session workspace (which IS writable/readable by me) or truncated with a summary, not dumped somewhere the calling agent cannot reach. I lost two round-trips to this and recovered only by abandoning the tool.

Second friction: government sites are the primary sources for this question and they are exactly what the fetch tooling handles worst. nist.gov/caisi, the NIST news index, and the ?k=CAISI search page all returned JS-rendered shells with no listings; the /news/2026/08 index 404'd. For a question that hinges on 'did agency X publish a press release in this 24-day window,' the highest-value tool would be a date-filtered press-release feed reader (GovDelivery bulletins, agency RSS, Federal Register API) rather than generic web search. I could see the May 5 GovDelivery bulletin URL in search results but had no way to enumerate that account's bulletins by date. A `federal_register_search` or `agency_press_releases(agency, date_range)` tool would have converted my central question from an inferential one into a lookup.

Third: recency-filtered search is missing. I wanted 'news published between 2026-08-10 and 2026-08-19' and had to fake it by stuffing literal date strings into queries, which mostly returned the same May and early-August articles. The absence of a date filter means I can never fully distinguish 'nothing happened' from 'search didn't surface it' — a real problem for a window-based question where absence of evidence is the primary evidence.

The prompt guided me well here. The Step 1b pre-publication check was directly load-bearing: the window start (Aug 10) precedes published_at (Aug 15), which is Case 1, and separately the dominant recent event (Aug 3-4) sits just outside the window — flagging that early stopped me from mistaking the framework finalization for a resolving event. The threshold-question guidance to model the quantity first mapped cleanly onto a hazard-rate decomposition rather than a narrative YES/NO argument, and the sensitivity grid confirmed the answer was robust rather than knife-edge. The instruction not to use the Agent tool unless requested was mildly costly — a parallel fan-out over the ~8 agency sites would have been the natural move for the 'did anything happen in the window' sweep.
